Known limitations

What this port does not do, what has not been tested, and what is known to be broken. Read it with README.md §"Security status", which lists what must change before production, and TEST_RESULTS.md, which records what has run on hardware.

Everything here is a current statement about the delivered code. DECISIONS.md holds the reasoning and the history.

1. Before production

The shipped configuration is a development configuration. README.md §"Security status" is the list; DESIGN.md §13 says how to address each item. In short: the signing keys are the public TF-M sample keys, provisioning supplies dummy HUK and IAK values, anti-rollback counters are left at 1, the clock and low-power registers are writable from the non-secure world, and the device lifecycle and secure debug are not enforced.

None of these is a defect in the port. They are the settings a development board needs and a product must not keep.

2. Crypto

Both parts route PSA crypto through FSP's Mbed TLS *_ALT sources, so what the hardware accelerates depends on the engine fitted to the part.

Accelerated

PartEngineAccelerated
RA6M5SCE9AES (128/192/256, ECB/CBC/CTR), AES-GCM, CMAC, SHA-256, ECP and ECDSA, RSA
RA8M2RSIP-E50Dthe same set, with the RSA key-generation exception below

BL2 also hashes images on the engine rather than in software.

In software, by choice

AES-CCM. FSP's SCE9 CCM caps associated data at 110 bytes and Protected Storage exceeds that, so CCM is built from software. It still reaches the engine block by block through the cipher and AES paths, so the cost is the mode logic rather than the block operation.

Unavailable

These are turned off in the accelerator configuration for both engines (platform/ext/accelerator/renesas/{sce9,rsip_e50d}/crypto_accelerator_config.h):

AlgorithmWhy
PSA_WANT_ALG_DETERMINISTIC_ECDSAneither engine implements RFC 6979. The attestation key signs with plain PSA_ALG_ECDSA. PSA Arch crypto test 252 skips for this reason
PSA_WANT_ECC_SECP_R1_521not supported by the engines
PSA_WANT_ECC_MONTGOMERY_255not supported by the engines

**RSA-2048 key generation in plaintext format is unavailable on RA8M2, and there is no switch for it.** The guard is in FSP's rsa_alt_process.c: mbedtls_rsa_gen_key() returns MBEDTLS_ERR_PLATFORM_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED unless the part is SCE7, SCE9 or RSIP-E51A, and E50D is not in that list. RA6M5 passes because SCE9 is. Every other RSA-2048 operation works on both parts. Hardware RSA key generation on E50D requires the caller to request a wrapped key. Raising PSA_CRYPTO_CFG_RSA_FORMAT does not help, because it is already 3 and is not what selects the failing path. This is the single PSA Arch crypto failure on RA8M2, test 216 check 4.

Untested

ECDSA P-384 is untested here and probably works. PSA_WANT_ECC_SECP_R1_384 is not disabled, so the algorithm is built, but the regression test that would exercise it (TFM_S_CRYPTO_TEST_1056 / TFM_NS_CRYPTO_TEST_1056) self-skips on every platform that is not Arm CryptoCell — its gate tests CC3XX_RUNTIME_ENABLED. The test reports PASSED without testing anything. Do not read a passing regression run as P-384 coverage. It needs a standalone check before anyone claims P-384 support.

The multi-part engine lock. While a multi-part AES, GCM or CMAC operation is open it holds the engine, and psa_generate_random fails for every caller until that operation completes or is aborted. This comes from reading the driver, not from an observed failure, and no suite run here exercises the pattern.

A software CTR defect no suite here can reach. FSP 6.7's mbedtls_aes_crypt_ctr() ignores nc_off and stream_block and mishandles partial blocks. PSA Arch tests 236 and 237 pass on both parts, short-input CTR checks included, because the PSA cipher layer never reaches that function with a partial block. A direct Mbed TLS CTR caller still hits it. Closing this needs a unit test against the function itself, not another PSA-level suite.

3. Boot and upgrade

The MCUboot upgrade path has been exercised on RA8M2 only. Both images install from their secondary slots and a second reset erases the secondary, under both toolchains. RA6M5 has no upgrade launch and the path has never run there. RA6E1 sets MCUBOOT_ALIGN_VAL to 128 to match its code-flash write unit, and that fix has never been exercised, because it only takes effect once BL2 writes code flash.

Image alignment is not interchangeable. Images signed at one alignment are rejected by a BL2 built at another, because the trailer magic differs. Reflash every slot after changing it and do not mix.

Slot order is reversed for image 0 on RA8M2. The secure secondary sits below the secure primary, so rsp.br_image_off of 0x68000 is the primary. Image 1 is the usual way round. Anything that reads a boot_rsp or computes a flash row must account for this.

Firmware Update is off and untested. TFM_PARTITION_FIRMWARE_UPDATE is OFF on all parts. Turning it on brings advisory TFMV-9 (CVE-2025-53022) into scope and you should move to TF-Mv2.2.2 first.

Measured boot is on, and a passing attestation suite does not prove it works. With no software components recorded, attest_add_all_sw_components() emits IAT_NO_SW_COMPONENTS and returns success, so the attestation suite passes either way. Read the boot record directly to confirm it.

4. Open hazards

Flashing a flat binary can destroy the board

The option-setting words live in discrete flash regions. A plain objcopy -O binary coalesces them into one segment and zero-fills the reserved bytes between, which writes 0x00 into defined option registers. Two EK-RA6M4 boards were lost this way; no recovery is known.

Flash bl2.hex or bl2.srec, never bl2.bin.

The full build re-emits a safe flat binary and verifies it, but **building the bl2_bin target on its own still writes the coalesced image.** The rule that follows is: build everything, never bl2_bin alone. If you must look at a flat binary, a safe one is tens of kilobytes and a coalesced one is about 16.8 MB. Do not use any single byte count as the test — the safe size differs between build configurations.

The debugger will program the TrustZone boundaries wrongly

Every launch configuration must keep com.renesas.hardwaredebug.arm.jlink.setTZBoundaries = false. Launched against BL2, the debugger derives the boundaries from the wrong symbols.

Five RA8M2 GCC launches carry the equivalent e2lite key as true. Their jlink key is false, so the setting is inert while J-Link is the selected probe. **Switching probe arms it.** The two Debug_SSD launches under e2_baseline/ keep the jlink key as true deliberately, because that directory shows e2's unmodified output; do not launch from it.

Re-partitioning erases the part

Programming the TrustZone boundaries with RDPM erases both code and data flash. Reflash all three images afterwards. RECONFIGURING_THE_LAYOUT.md is the procedure.

The secure slot is nearly full

RA6M5 has about 1.7 KB spare and RA8M2 about 0.7 KB, measured against the signed payload rather than the raw image. Enabling a diagnostic option that costs a few kilobytes will fail to link. README.md §"Freeing space in the secure image" gives the measured cost of each.

5. Debug and logging

RTT is unreliable across the boot chain by construction. BL2, the secure image and the non-secure image each initialise their own RTT control block, and the address differs per build. A capture can also truncate silently: if output stops after a result line and the next test is never announced, suspect the capture rather than the target.

Most launches do not load what the build scripts produce. Four do, one per part and toolchain: ra6m5_TFM_sce9_{gcc,iar} and ra8m2_TFM_app_{gcc,iar}, whose load entries are the default build directories of the four application scripts. Every other launch names a build tree of its own by absolute path, so running an application build and then one of those flashes different images or fails on missing files. GETTING_STARTED.md §6 has the table.

All nineteen RA6M5 launches additionally take their debug program from the e2 project — Debug/ra6m5_gcc_nonsecure.elf — rather than from a TF-M image, so the symbols e2 loads are not those of the image being flashed. The fifteen RA8M2 launches name a bl2.elf instead.

6. Platform scope

PartStatus
RA6M5supported, both toolchains
RA8M2supported, both toolchains. CPU1 is unused; the port is single-core
RA6E1reference only. It is the port the two supported parts derive from, and it is not maintained against the current build

RA6M4 is not part of this delivery.

The RA8M2 project sets target different board revisions between toolchains. The GCC projects select ra8m2_ek and the IAR projects ra8m2_ek_v2. Both have passed on hardware, so the difference is tolerable, but regenerating either set against the other's board changes the generated BSP. The RA6M5 projects differ similarly in pin configuration: the GCC solution selects RA6M5_2 CK and the IAR solution RA6M5 CK, which changes the security attribution of 16 pins.

7. Planned work

Listed without dates, because none is committed.

  • Mbed TLS v4 and TF-M 2.3. Gated on FSP's own migration to Mbed TLS v4.1. The port stays on TF-Mv2.2.0 and Mbed TLS 3.6.3 until then.
  • Move the project set to RASC. The delivered projects are generated by e2 studio. The standalone FSP Smart Configurator emits an equivalent CMake project set, and the layout and module configuration already match on RA6M5. What is not yet solved is the debug front end: RASC projects cannot be imported into e2 studio, and their own launch mechanism has not been shown to flash three images with the required erase and boundary settings.
  • Firmware Update. The bootloader half is proven on RA8M2; what FWU adds is the API that places an image in the secondary slot.
  • SLIH above isolation 1, and on RA8M2 at all. Never run. The trees and launches have to be made first.
  • PSA Arch Firmware Framework suite. Only the crypto, attestation and storage suites have been built.
